newsitem.title: GERMANY: German stock watchdog shies at strict insider rule.
newsitem.headline: German stock watchdog shies at strict insider rule.

text.p: Germany's securities watchdog, the BAWe, on Wednesday appeared to shy away from a strict definition of insider trading, as its president said certain uses of privileged market information may not be illegal.

In an interview with the Handelsblatt newspaper, Georg Wittich said the decisive factor in deciding whether to punish insider trading was the degree of impact the transactions had on the price of the stock involved.

"If the price move remains below the threshold of what might be termed considerable, then it is not an insider trade," Wittich told the newspaper, adding that the information which sparked such a stock move would be regarded as "confidential information," not "insider information."
A price change would only be regarded as "considerable" if it exceeded "the normal fluctuation band", Wittich said.
The Handelsblatt interpreted Wittich's comments as a green light for brokers to engage in insider dealing.
Wittich himself was unavailable for comment on the article but Werner Seifert, head of the German Stock Exchange, later told a news conference that the BAWe president had been misinterpreted.

"That is not the Wittich we know," he said, adding that the BAWe and local stock market supervisors would continue to examine all transactions conducted on German exchanges and would follow up any suspicions of insider dealing.
The two-year-old BAWe's central task is eliminating insider trading in Germany, after insider deals were criminalised for the first time by a law passed mid-1994.

The agency monitors hundreds of thousands of transactions daily to catch any aberrations, has investigated dozens of cases of suspected insider deals and has been instrumental in Germany's first ever prosecutions for such offences.
Current German securities law allows penalties of up to five years in jail for insider trading.

A piece of insider information is described in German law as "every fact that is not yet publicly known .... which is capable of having a considerable effect on the price of the insider security, should it be announced publicly."
